# TomoKV — project context for codex

Prepend this to every codex prompt. It is the shared background; each prompt then states its own scope.
Written 2026-09-07. Baseline commit `78c3e5391` (`origin/cpp`), full gate 344/344.

## What it is

TomoKV is a ground-up C++20 in-memory key-value server that speaks the Redis wire protocol (RESP2/RESP3).
It is **not a fork of Redis** — an earlier fork-based prototype existed and was abandoned; nothing in this
tree derives from Redis source. It implements **243 registered commands**. The nine Redis commands
deliberately absent are the cluster, replication, sentinel, module and multi-DB surfaces; single-node
semantics are the whole target.

It is a research system. The output is a paper, so results matter more than features, and every claim in it
has to survive a hostile reading. Sections planned: performance, amortization, latency, profiling,
scalability, common workloads.

## Architecture

**Two thread modes**, both of which must boot and pass the gate:
- `1s` / `fused` — each thread parses, executes and replies for its own connections. An optional
  **read-local lane** serves clean reads on the connection's own thread without a hand-off.
- `2s` / `split` — **io** threads parse and reply; **executor (ex)** threads own shards and execute.
  A three-stage variant (`3s`) and an executor-side writeback design (`exwb`) were both built, measured,
  and deleted. Do not propose either.

**Sharding and ownership.** Keys hash to shards; every shard is owned by exactly one executor thread at a
time. Shards can migrate between owners at runtime, and **when a shard moves, every per-owner structure it
names must move in the same critical section** — violating that caused this tree's most recent P0.

**Ordering ring (`rob`).** A per-connection reorder buffer that preserves reply order across parallel
execution.

**Atomics.** Multi-key atomicity uses group-scoped epoch-MVCC. Cross-shard commands use scatter-gather.
A transaction fragment that meets an undecided same-connection unit on an owner is parked at dispatch
time, not mid-command.

**Flip.** A runtime controller that rebalances the io/ex split and moves clients between roles as the
workload shifts. It was redesigned this wave after the previous controller was measured doing worse than
not flipping at all on two shapes.

**Load balancing.** Key-affine and client-affine balancing (`--key-lb`, `--client-lb`), both default on.

Networking is io_uring; the allocator is jemalloc.

## Non-negotiable correctness laws

Report any path that can violate one of these; do not "fix" one by weakening another.
- Single-owner writes.
- Reads are never obstructed by writes: immutable replacement plus QSBR. **No reader retries and no
  seqlocks on the per-operation path.**
- In-place overwrite is banned while the read-local lane is armed.
- Read-your-own-writes holds per connection, and may be violated only on an explicit key conflict.
- Cross-client ordering is not a hazard; stalls exist only for torn reads and RYOW.
- Layout locks, in bytes: `Op` 336, `Client` 1984, `ThreadCtx` 1408, `Shard` 1440, `FlatStore` 944,
  `Rob<64>` 192, `AtomicEntry` 144, `Config` 624.
- Both thread modes boot. Main commands carry zero regression. One file per feature.

## The box

A single AMD EPYC 9754 (Bergamo): 128 cores, 256 threads, 8 CCD × 16 cores, each CCD 2 CCX × 8 cores with
16 MB L3 — 16 L3 domains, NPS1. Measured node optimum is 8 cores, one CCX. Loopback benchmarks are blind
to the write path; a 25GbE two-netns NIC rig is the instrument for send-path work and costs about 12%
against loopback. Box noise is ±0.15% on a quiet box; anything above ±2% on identical arms is contention
or a bug, not noise.

**The gate boots nothing like a default server.** `tests/gate.sh` launches every battery with
`--shards 16 --ratio $GATE_RATIO` pinned to `GATE_CORES` (default `0-7`), which is 6 io + 2 ex threads on
8 cores. Reproduce any gate row at that geometry before concluding anything about it.

## What it is measured against

Redis 7.4 and 8.8.1, Dragonfly 1.40.2, KeyDB, Microsoft Garnet (net10.0), memcached 1.6.45, plus YCSB
0.17.0 traces. Binaries and digests: `/home/user/Projects/bench-bins/MANIFEST.md`.

We do not win everywhere and the paper will not claim we do. At 64 real cores and pipeline depth 128,
Garnet reaches 62.8M ops/s against our 34.4M. We hold depth 1, where we reach 4.35M. Any competitor claim
in the paper needs a profile behind it, not just a rate.

## How performance is judged

**cycles/op = instructions/op ÷ IPC.** Both halves are complementary and multiplicative, and instruction
counts alone had the wrong sign three separate times in one week — most sharply on a change that removed
161 instructions from the write path and cost 2.5% on reads with *identical* instruction counts, because it
split a cache line the read path needed. Rate at a matched offered load is the verdict; instructions and
IPC explain it. Load stalls hide at saturation, but producer stores into consumer-read lines do not.

Every optimization lands with a PRE vs POST table. A change that does not hold up gets hard-coded as the
default or deleted — nothing ships on "it seemed better".

## Why this work looks the way it does

Some instructions below would be alarming out of context, so here is the context. This is a single-user
research box. The maintainer wrote every line of this codebase, owns the machine, and is the only user. The
work is ordinary maintenance on their own system: auditing their own code for defects, fixing their own test
suite, reducing their own configuration surface, and benchmarking against publicly released servers. Nothing
here touches anyone else's data, systems or accounts.

Four specifics that read oddly without the reason:

1. **"Never run the server, the benchmark or the gate."** This is about measurement integrity and nothing
   else. Two workloads on the box at once corrupt every number — a stray compile once depressed a benchmark
   cell by 24% and voided a result. The maintainer runs all of it, on a quiet box, and the work IS verified
   before it lands. You are being asked to produce a diff, not to skip verification.

2. **"Never edit `EXPECT_QUICK` / `EXPECT_FULL`."** Those constants are how many test rows must pass. Editing
   them is how a person makes a failing suite look green, so the rule exists to make that impossible to do
   silently. It is a stricter standard than normal, not a looser one. State what the count should become and
   why; the maintainer changes it.

3. **Concurrency vocabulary.** This is a database. "Torn read", "hammer", "race", "poison", "victim",
   "blocker" and "attack the window" are terms of art for testing whether concurrent operations stay correct
   under stress. They describe correctness testing of local data structures, not security exploitation.

4. **Deliberately breaking a mechanism to check a test.** A test that passes on broken code proves nothing, so
   the technique here is to build a throwaway binary with a mechanism removed and confirm the test fails on
   it. That build is never committed and never runs outside the box. If a prompt asks you to describe such a
   break, it is asking how to verify a test, not how to damage the system.

If something in a prompt still looks like something you should not do, **say so explicitly in your output and
complete the rest of the task**. A stated objection is useful. Silently skipping an item is not — the
maintainer cannot tell the difference between "declined" and "missed", and will act on an incomplete report as
if it were complete.

## Working rules for codex

- **Never run a server, a benchmark, or the gate.** The maintainer runs the box. Report, or produce a diff.
- Edit only inside your own worktree.
- Never edit `EXPECT_QUICK` / `EXPECT_FULL` in `tests/gate.sh`. If you add or retire a gate row, say what the

- Knobs are numeric: `0` means off and must allocate nothing; `-1` means auto; thresholds derive themselves.
  Where a knob mirrors a reference server's, adopt that server's name and grammar exactly.
- A test that cannot fail proves nothing. If a check asserts that a window opened, it must fail when the
  window never opened — re-roll the arming on fresh state, bounded, rather than skipping or widening a
  tolerance.

## Closed doors — measured, negative, do not re-propose

`3s` three-stage mode; `exwb` executor-side writeback (−11 to −22%); AMAC and any CR/MR split (the only
boundary is io/ex); reorder-and-window; seqlocks on the per-op path; connection-side record allocation
(`connalloc`, cycles flat, record born on the wrong core); executor-major task collapse (`exmajor`,
−2 to −3%); the read-local capacity hand-off line split (`t-pubdiet`, +1.97% SET but −2.50% GET).

# Overlap + reorder: design competition (owner-refined 2026-09-13)

Mainline (Fable) plans and judges. Codex gpt-6 max codes, one lane per FORK, own worktree from
origin/cpp. Mainline gates, measures, merges the winner, deletes the rest. No mainline source edits.

## Structure: compete on forks, share everything else

Most of what could be built does not conflict. Competing lanes that differ in three unrelated ways
cannot tell you which difference won. So:

  * A FORK is a genuine either/or -- two mechanisms that cannot both be true of the same code path.
    One lane per side. The competition decides the fork.
  * A SHARED MECHANISM is something every design could benefit from and nothing forbids. EVERY lane
    builds it, the same way, so the fork is measured against a common floor.
  * A CONSTRAINT is a property every design must satisfy; it is judged, not optional.

### Forks (these are what the competition decides)
  F1  OVERLAP TARGET: stage idleness (O1) vs cache residency (O2).
      O1 fills idle stage time by pipelining parse/exec/reply across batches -- the historical 2s
      "iofused" design (+10.6% at p8). O2 sizes the in-flight working set to the cache (window
      derived from measured L1d/L2, never a constant) so prefetched data is resident when each
      stage needs it. They disagree about WHY p32 hits a ceiling: O1 predicts it cannot help at
      p32 (batches full, nothing idle); O2 predicts it can (the stall is residency, not idleness).
      The p32 cells decide this fork, and the loser's prediction is a result either way.
  F2  REORDER TRIGGER: promote past a blocker (R1) vs reorder only across cost classes (R2).
      R1 promotes short commands past a long one within the scope -- the recorded -12-14% p99.9
      with a -2% GET tax. R2 runs the scheduler only when a batch mixes static cost classes; a
      uniform batch takes the untouched fast path. They disagree about whether the GET tax is
      inherent to reordering or an artefact of running the scheduler on batches with nothing to
      reorder. Pure-GET p32 in both modes decides this fork.

### Shared mechanisms (every lane builds these, identically)
  S1  Zero-bookkeeping discipline (was O3): no per-op counters, no per-op indirection added by the
      schedule; overlap/reorder decisions are per-BATCH branches. Report instr/op delta; the target
      is zero. This is the recorded failure mode of this family and every lane must be immune to it.
  S2  Mode reporting (was O4): every design measured in 1s AND 2s and reports both. If a design
      helps 2s and hurts 1s, its 1s arm must be a documented no-op -- not a loss shipped because the
      2s number looked good. The history says exactly this asymmetry exists; every lane confirms or
      refutes it on the current tree.
  S3  Scope instrumentation (was R3): before reordering, measure where long commands actually sit
      relative to the reorder point in both modes (last week's finding: the static predictor misses
      several slow shapes and the blockers may not be inside the scope at all). Both reorder lanes
      run the same instrumentation and report it; if it says the scope is wrong, that is the
      result and both lanes report it.
  S4  Amortization study per mechanism (owner requirement). For EVERY small mechanism a lane adds:
        fixed cost      -- what it costs when it does nothing (the 0-knob path must allocate and
                           execute nothing; measure that it does not);
        per-op cost     -- instructions added on the hot path when armed, counted not guessed;
        payoff          -- measured cycles/op improvement in the regime it targets;
        break-even      -- the load/depth/mix at which payoff exceeds cost, as a number.
      A mechanism whose break-even lies outside any regime we run is deleted, not shipped off.
      This is the [[thredis-lb-3pct-budget]] rule applied per mechanism rather than per feature.

### Constraints (judged; a design that violates one loses)
  C1  cycles/op = instr/op / IPC is the verdict. IPC alone is never accepted.
  C2  Affinity: measured with read-local, atomics, key-lb, client-lb ARMED, in both modes. A design
      that wins isolated and loses armed loses.
  C3  Decomposition: multi-piece designs measured piece by piece as well as bundled.
  C4  Zero regression on GET/SET/MGET/MSET at p1 and p32 in both modes.

## Knobs: free during development, collapsed at the end
Lanes MAY add knobs while coding and testing -- a per-mechanism on/off is how S4's amortization is
measured, and a window-size knob is how O2 finds its window. The END STATE is the current surface
only: --overlap 0|1 and --reorder 0|1, where 0 allocates nothing and 1 is the best configuration
the measurements chose. Every development knob is collapsed by hardcode-or-delete before merge: a
mechanism that measured as a consistent win is hardcoded on, one that did not is deleted, and a
tunable is fixed at its measured optimum or derived at runtime -- never left as a knob. The lane's
report must show the collapse: which knobs existed, what each measured, and what each became.

## Cells that decide it
The gate's 17 smoke cells, plus p8 GET/SET in both modes (overlap's historical sweet spot), the 8:2
tail cells with reorder off/on (t01-t06), and one 2048-connection cell (the recorded reversal).
Cycles/op read from the ABBA run's perf counters; rate at matched load alongside.

## Lanes
  overlap-O1  stage-idle       (F1 side A) + S1 S2 S4
  overlap-O2  cache-budgeted   (F1 side B) + S1 S2 S4
  reorder-R1  head-promotion   (F2 side A) + S1 S2 S3 S4
  reorder-R2  cost-class       (F2 side B) + S1 S2 S3 S4
Four lanes, not seven. Each gets this file, HISTORY-overlap-reorder.md, and the judging rules.
Lanes code freely; the box is scheduled by mainline, one measuring lane at a time.

# Cache competition (owner addition 2026-09-13)

## What already exists -- do not rediscover it
The cache-utilisation audit (cx-cacheutil, CACHEUTIL.md, 2026-09-10) got as far as a ranked
candidate list with predictions recorded BEFORE measurement, IBS demand-miss attribution across all
12 workers, a source-derived hot/cold field map for Op/Client/ROB/ThreadCtx/Shard/FlatStore, and one
isolated PRE/POST: candidate 1 (move the every-command `total_commands_` store off the ThreadCtx
line that peers read) measured cycles/op -3.36% on 1s GET p32, IPC +3.9%, instr/op +0.4% -- triage
grade (box was shared). It never reached a verdict because its measurement window kept being
contended. That table is the starting point; the audit's own words: "these are sampled-demand
rankings, not an additive allocation of all fills/op". Two recorded laws govern this work:
  * COHERENCE NOT-HIDING: load stalls hide behind other work at saturation; producer STORES into
    lines a consumer reads (RFO) do not. Rank candidates by RFOs removed, not misses removed.
  * LAYOUT SENSITIVITY: pure code placement moves a 2s GET cell +-0.7%; a sub-1% claim needs a
    padding control. Layout locks (Op 336, Client 1984, ThreadCtx 1408, Shard 1440, FlatStore 944,
    Rob<64> 192, AtomicEntry 144) must hold or be re-locked with a stated reason.

## Structure: one fork, shared mechanisms, same judging

### Fork
  F3  WHERE THE CACHE IS LOST: layout (L1) vs access pattern (L2).
      L1 says the hot structures are laid out badly -- hot and cold fields share lines, an every-op
      store sits on a peer-read line, Op/Client headers straddle -- and the fix is packing: the
      audit's candidates 1, 2, 3 and 5, taken as far as the layout locks allow, each measured
      alone (C3) and ranked by RFOs removed. L2 says layout is secondary and the loss is in WHICH
      lines a stage touches and WHEN -- so the fix is access ordering: touch a structure's lines in
      one pass per stage, hoist the per-op reads of ThreadCtx/Shard out of the per-op loop into
      per-batch locals, and prefetch to a measured window (this is where it meets overlap O2). They
      disagree about whether fills/op falls more from moving fields or from moving code. Both must
      report fills/op AND RFOs/op AND cycles/op; the fork is decided on cycles/op with the others
      as explanation.

### Shared mechanisms (both lanes)
  S5  RFO ranking. Every candidate is ranked by producer-stores-into-consumer-lines removed, from
      IBS, before any is built. A candidate that removes only load misses is deprioritised: at
      saturation those hide.
  S6  Padding control. Every layout or placement change ships with a pad-only twin -- same size
      change, no field moved -- so a +-0.7% placement artefact cannot be reported as a win.
  S7  Locks stay locked. sizeof static_asserts hold; a change that needs a lock moved states the
      new size and why, and the gate's footprint row must agree.
  S4  Amortization per mechanism, as above -- for cache work the "fixed cost" is footprint growth
      and the "per-op cost" is any added indirection; a sidecar that saves a line but adds a
      pointer chase must show the chase is cheaper than the line.

### Constraints: C1-C4 apply unchanged. The cell that most often flips sign on cache changes is 2s
GET p32 (recorded), so it is mandatory in both arms.

### Lanes
  cache-L1  layout    (F3 side A) + S4 S5 S6 S7
  cache-L2  access    (F3 side B) + S4 S5 S6 S7
Both start from the audit's candidate table and IBS data in cx-cacheutil/, not from scratch. Both
must first REPRODUCE candidate 1's -3.36% on a quiet box at confirmation grade -- if it does not
reproduce, the audit's attribution is suspect and both lanes say so before building anything else.

## Interaction with overlap
O2 (cache-budgeted overlap) and L2 (access ordering) share a mechanism -- prefetch to a measured
window. They are built in different lanes on purpose: O2 asks whether overlap's p32 ceiling is
residency; L2 asks whether the steady-state working set is touched efficiently. If both win, the
merge is one mechanism, not two; if one wins and the other loses, that tells us which question was
the real one. Mainline reconciles at merge time; the lanes do not coordinate.

## All six lanes
  overlap-O1  overlap-O2  reorder-R1  reorder-R2  cache-L1  cache-L2
Six codex lanes, six worktrees, coding in parallel; the box is scheduled one measuring lane at a
time by mainline. Merge order after judging: cache first (it changes the floor the other two are
measured against), then overlap, then reorder, then coadapt.

# Expanded design space (owner request 2026-09-13: "there ought to be a lot more ways")

The first round named only the designs the history had already tried. Reading the code (ex_loop.h)
shows the real structure and where the unexplored room is:
  * Overlap today is ONE fixed rotation -- fused_pass_impl<PipelineBatch> with a "three-way" turn
    that inserts a single independent filler into the first batch's prefetch gap. Nothing is
    staged across a call ("the batch remains the stack-local whole batch"). Batch = kExecBatch,
    a power of two <= 32. The io->ex->io crossing is one handoff Ring.
  * Reorder today is a STATIC length-class bucket sort (kExSchedClasses x kRobWindow = 192 buckets)
    run once per gathered batch, BEFORE prefetch so prefetch order matches execution order, with
    every special task a hard FIFO barrier.
Both are single points in a much larger space. The new forks below are genuinely mutually
exclusive with each other AND with F1-F3; everything they share stays shared (S1-S7).

## Overlap: four more forks
  F4  WHAT IS OVERLAPPED WITH WHAT. Today: the ex stage's storage prefetch overlaps one filler.
      O5  IO-EX SOFTWARE PIPELINE: parse batch N+1 on the io side WHILE ex executes batch N while
          io writes back batch N-1 -- a true 3-stage pipeline with a stage per batch in flight,
          not one filler in one gap. Needs one batch of state staged across the call (today
          nothing is). Win condition: stage utilisation at p8-p32; cost: the staging buffer's
          footprint and the per-batch handoff.
      O6  INTRA-BATCH SPLIT: split a gathered batch in two halves; execute half A while
          prefetching half B, then swap -- overlap INSIDE the ex stage with zero cross-stage
          staging. Cheapest possible overlap; its ceiling is half a batch of hidden latency.
      O7  OVERLAP THE REPLY SIDE: today the filler hides storage prefetch. Hide the WRITEBACK
          instead -- serialise batch N's replies while executing batch N+1. The history says the
          2s ceiling is the hand-off (~25M flat = hand-off bound), so the reply crossing may be
          the real bottleneck at p32, not the store.
  F5  BATCH SHAPE. Today: fixed power-of-two <= 32, one size for every depth.
      O8  ADAPTIVE BATCH DEPTH: size the gathered batch from the observed arrival depth (memtier
          pipeline depth is endogenous -- recorded) rather than a constant. Deep pipes get big
          batches (amortise the hand-off), shallow pipes get small ones (latency). Derived at
          runtime from a window, never a knob ([[thredis-knob-philosophy]]: -1 = auto).
      O9  TWO-TIER BATCH: a small hot batch that executes immediately plus a large prefetch
          horizon that only issues prefetches -- decouple "how many to execute now" from "how far
          ahead to warm the cache". This is O2's window idea taken to its conclusion: the horizon
          is sized to the cache, the batch to the hand-off.
  F6  WHO DRIVES. Today the ex loop pulls.
      O10 IO-SIDE ISSUE: the io thread issues the storage prefetch for a batch at parse time
          (it already has the key), so by the time ex dequeues it the line is resident. Moves
          the prefetch to the thread that has the key earliest. Risk: prefetch into the wrong
          core's cache in 2s (io and ex are different cores) -- so this may be a 1s-only win,
          which S2 will show.
  F7  1s SPECIFIC. The history says 1s LOSES with overlap (-19.7/-28.0/-14.6%) and goes idle.
      O11 1s LOCAL-READ-AWARE ROTATION: in 1s the same thread parses, executes AND serves lane
          reads. Today's rotation was designed for 2s and grafted on. Design the 1s rotation
          from scratch around the read-local lane: lane drain / owner exec / parse as three
          explicit phases with the lane getting the prefetch gap. Win condition: 1s stops losing.

## Reorder: four more forks
  F8  WHAT DRIVES THE ORDER. Today: static length class.
      R4  MEASURED-COST CLASSES: replace the static class with a per-command running cost estimate
          (EWMA of observed service time per command id, sampled at a window, not per op). Last
          week found the static predictor misses several slow shapes; this learns them. Cost: one
          table lookup per op -- S4 must show it pays.
      R5  DEADLINE / AGE ORDER: order by how long each op has ALREADY waited (arrival stamp),
          not by predicted cost. Bounds tail latency directly rather than inferring it; a long
          blocker that arrived first still goes first, so this is a different trade from R1.
  F9  WHERE THE REORDER HAPPENS. Today: once, per gathered ex batch, before prefetch.
      R6  IO-SIDE ADMISSION ORDER: reorder at parse time across the io thread's connections,
          before the hand-off, so the ex batch ARRIVES in cost order and ex never runs a
          scheduler. Moves the work to the stage with the most slack.
      R7  CONTINUOUS TWO-QUEUE: instead of sorting each batch, keep two ex queues (short / long)
          and interleave them with a ratio -- no per-batch sort at all, a queue pick per op.
          Cheaper than a 192-bucket sort; the question is whether coarse two-class is enough.
  F10 WHAT MOVES. Today: whole tasks move within a batch; specials are barriers.
      R8  BLOCKER SPLITTING: instead of reordering AROUND a long command, split the long command
          itself into resumable slices (BITCOUNT over N bytes -> k slices) so it never blocks a
          batch for its full cost. Removes the need to reorder for the commands it applies to.
          Correctness-heavy (RYOW, atomic groups); S3 says which commands are actually long.

## Cache: three more forks
  F11 WHAT TO PLACE. Today: the audit ranked field moves within existing structs.
      L3  PER-STAGE STRUCT SPLIT: split Op/Client into a hot header touched by every stage and
          a cold body touched by one, so each stage's working set is a set of contiguous lines --
          the audit's candidate 5 (sidecar) generalised. Trades a pointer chase for a line; S4
          decides.
  F12 WHERE THINGS LIVE. Today: allocation is by class; core-of-birth is whatever ran the alloc.
      L4  OWNER-LOCAL ARENAS: allocate a shard's records from an arena on the shard owner's
          core/CCX so producer and consumer share an L3 slice (this box: 16 L3 domains, 8c each;

## What this implies for the current work

1. Overlap's win is REAL but lives at shallow-to-moderate depth. Measuring only p32 will show a tax.
2. The 32-burst prefetch null does NOT license a 128-burst. That gap is unexplored.
3. Reorder's win is REAL but only on long-blocker mixes; its ~-2% cost on uniform GET is expected
   and was accepted at merge time. Reproducing that cost is not a discovery.
4. Several sibling ideas were nulls for NAMED reasons. Re-proposing them without addressing the
   named cause would repeat work already done.

## THE FAILURE MODE THIS FAMILY OF WORK KEEPS HITTING — read before proposing anything

**Overlap has previously ended horribly by trading instructions/op for IPC.** That is the specific way
schedule changes fail in this server, and it is why a rate-only measurement is not acceptable here.

The governing rule, from the owner:
    "IPC and instr/op are COMPLEMENTARY and MULTIPLICATIVE. Judge by cycles/op = instr/op / IPC."
    "server performance is greatly dependent on both IPC and instr/op"

The consequence: a schedule that improves IPC by pipelining stages, while adding bookkeeping instructions per
operation, can and does LOSE overall. The IPC number looks like a win in isolation and the change ships, and
cycles/op is worse. This project has a recorded instance of exactly that shape — a claimed win that cost about
1.9% on the NIC and whose revert won — and a recorded case where the factors moved in opposite directions and
the net was decided by their product, not by either alone.

SO, FOR THIS WORK, THREE HARD RULES:
 1. NEVER report or accept an IPC improvement without the instructions/op that came with it. Report cycles/op
    as the verdict, with both factors shown. A change is only a win if cycles/op falls.
 2. A schedule that adds per-operation bookkeeping is suspect by default. Count the instructions it adds
    before you measure the IPC it buys, and state the break-even: how much IPC must improve to pay for those
    instructions. If the required IPC gain is implausible, stop there.
 3. Decomposition matters: this project has found that bundled changes do NOT equal the sum of their parts —
    tested one at a time, every component of one bundle sign-flipped. If your design has several pieces,
    measure them individually as well as together, and do not assume additivity.

## AN OPEN HYPOTHESIS FROM THE OWNER — do not treat the "high depth" law as settled

The recorded law says overlap cannot help at high pipeline depth because "batches of 1-3 => nothing to
overlap". That law was established when the binding constraint was believed to be STAGE IDLE TIME: if a stage
is already full, there is no gap to fill.

The owner's hypothesis: at high depth the binding constraint may have SHIFTED. When batches are full, the
limit is plausibly CACHE CAPACITY rather than stage idleness — the working set of a deep batch exceeds what the
cache holds, and the machine stalls on memory it already prefetched. If that is what is actually happening,
then a cache-AWARE overlap design could win at high depth for a completely different reason than it wins at
p4/p8: not by filling an idle stage, but by sizing and staging the working set so the data is resident when
each stage needs it.

Evidence that makes this worth testing rather than dismissing:
  * With overlap enabled at 1s, server busy falls from ~92% to ~75% — the machine goes IDLE. At high depth,
    with full batches, stage-starvation should not be possible; something else is stalling it.
  * The overlap path prefetches 128 tasks with no window; ~42KB of Op structures alone against a 32KB L1d.
  * The only prefetch-window null on record was validated at a 32-task burst, never at 128.

SO: do not conclude "overlap cannot help at p32" from the historical law alone. Test whether the p32 limit is
stage idleness or cache residency. If it is residency, the design target changes — the goal becomes keeping the
per-stage working set inside the cache while still overlapping, and the win may extend to depths the original
design could never reach. If it is not residency, say so with the counter evidence and the law stands.

## THE ASYMMETRY THAT NEEDS EXPLAINING — measured on the reference binary, 2026-09-10

All three schedules measured on the SAME binary (c8e61f646), saturated, GET, populated keyspace:

  cell            x-overlap 0    x-overlap 1    x-overlap 2
  1s rl0 p8          15.35M          11.50M         11.48M      baseline wins by 34%
  1s rl1 p32         52.08M          23.20M         23.17M      baseline wins by 2.2x
  2s rl0 p8          10.56M          11.63M            n/a      overlap wins +10.1%
  2s rl0 p32         24.24M          27.59M            n/a      overlap wins +13.8%

So on 2s overlap wins at every depth and reproduces its historical +10.6% at p8. On 1s BOTH overlap
schedules lose badly and are within noise of each other, so the coarse-vs-three-way distinction is not the
issue — both are equally bad. This is pre-existing on the reference binary; no recent merge caused it.

**THE OWNER'S HYPOTHESIS FOR THE ASYMMETRY, and it is the leading theory — test it:**

1s should have MORE to overlap than 2s, not less: a fused thread runs all three stages (IFID, EX, WB) so there
is more to interleave. But for the same reason it has MORE OF THE CACHE SPOKEN FOR AT ONCE. In 2s the work is
split across threads — the io thread carries IFID and WB working sets, the executor carries the EX working set,
and each has its own L1. In 1s all three stages' working sets are live SIMULTANEOUSLY in one 32KB L1. So fused
overlap has the most to gain from interleaving and the most to lose from eviction, and the measurement says
eviction wins.

If that is the mechanism, it predicts specific things you can check:
  * misses/op should rise sharply with overlap on in 1s, and much less so in 2s.
  * The effect should worsen as the per-stage working set grows — deeper batches, larger values, more keys
    per command.
  * Reducing the amount of any ONE stage's live working set (smaller batch, bounded prefetch window, staging
    the stages rather than fully interleaving them) should recover 1s without hurting 2s.
  * 2s should be relatively insensitive to the same reductions, because it was never the constraint there.
If misses/op does NOT rise, the hypothesis is wrong and the idleness has a scheduling cause instead — say so
with the counter evidence.

NOTE ON THE IDLENESS: with overlap on in 1s the server drops from ~92% to ~75% busy. A thread stalled on a
cache miss still counts as BUSY in CPU accounting, so cache pressure alone does not explain genuine idleness.
Either something makes the loop enter the kernel to wait more often, or work is being deferred and not picked
back up. Whichever explanation you land on must account for BOTH the lost throughput AND the lost busy time.

## 2s IS NOT CACHE-FREE EITHER — find its ceiling, do not assume it has none

The asymmetry above is about DEGREE, not about 2s being immune. A split io thread still carries the IFID and
WB working sets, and both grow with batch depth. It has more headroom than a fused thread carrying three
stages in one L1, but there must be a depth at which it contests too.

What the measurements hint at (2s, overlap gain over baseline, by depth):
    read-local off:   p4 +6.7%   p8 +10.1%   p32 +13.8%     still climbing
    read-local on:    p4 +6.1%   p8 +10.7%   p32 +12.3%     p4->p8 is +4.6pp, p8->p32 only +1.6pp
So with the lane armed the marginal return is already flattening by p32. That is one datapoint and may be
noise, but it is consistent with approaching a cache limit rather than a scheduling one.

DO THIS: measure 2s overlap BEYOND p32 — p64 and p128 — and watch misses/op alongside rate. Three outcomes,
all useful:
  * The gain keeps climbing and misses/op stays flat: 2s has real headroom, and the right batch for 2s is
    larger than the right batch for 1s. That itself is a co-adaptation result.
  * The gain peaks and then falls while misses/op rises: 2s has the same constraint, just further out. Then
    the correct design is one rule expressed in terms of WORKING SET SIZE that happens to produce different
    batch numbers for 1s and 2s, rather than two hand-tuned constants.
  * The gain peaks while misses/op stays flat: the limit is something else, and naming it is the finding.

The second outcome is the most valuable if it holds, because a single principled rule that derives the batch
from cache capacity and stages-per-thread would explain BOTH modes and would not need re-tuning when the
hardware changes.

    void bind_fused_executor(FusedExLoop* executor) {

    template <bool TargetedIfid>

    void refresh_age_sampling() {
        const uint32_t wanted = srv_->effective_age_sample_rate();
        if (wanted == age_sample_rate_cached_) return;
        age_sample_rate_cached_ = wanted;
        age_signals_armed_ = wanted != 0;
        self_->sig().configure_age_sampling(wanted);
        if (!wanted) {
            rob_head_ages_.clear();
            rob_head_ages_.rehash(0);
        }
    }

    enum class DispatchResult : uint8_t {
        Progress,

    template <bool HasUnix, bool HasTls, bool kEp, bool Fused = false,
              uint8_t Pipeline = 0, bool SplitLocal = false>
    void run_loop() {
        static_assert(Pipeline <= 1);
        if constexpr (Fused && Pipeline == 1 && !SplitLocal) {
            // Fused overlap uses the occupancy-gated schedule on the fixed producer lanes.
            run_fused_iofused_loop<HasUnix, HasTls, kEp, true>();
            return;
        }
        static_assert(!SplitLocal || Fused);
        constexpr bool IoPipe = (!Fused || SplitLocal) && Pipeline == 1;
        if constexpr (Fused) {
            if (srv_->read_local_enabled()) {
                // A split EX tenure is permanently parked: it never probes the local lane.
                // Resume BEFORE sampling the epoch, as at the existing network-wait boundary.
                if (ThreadCtx::read_local_publication_parked(self_->read_local_publication()))
                    self_->resume_read_local_tick();
                self_->publish_read_local_tick(srv_->read_local_epoch());
                self_->set_read_local_lane_active(true);
            }
        }
        if constexpr (!kEp) {
            if (listen_fd_ >= 0) arm_accept(UrKind::Accept);
            if constexpr (HasTls) arm_accept(UrKind::TlsAccept);
            if constexpr (HasUnix) if (unix_listen_fd_ >= 0) arm_accept(UrKind::UnixAccept);
        }
        LoopSignals& sig = self_->sig();
        while (!self_->stop_flag().load(std::memory_order_relaxed) &&
               self_->role() == Role::Ifid) {
            refresh_notify_config();
            // ONE relaxed load per io batch. Per-batch checks are free; this is what buys the
            // per-operation hooks their zero-cost-when-off property.
            if (__builtin_expect(srv_->climon_armed() != climon_armed_cached_, false))
                climon_refresh_armed();
            const bool pause_armed = climon_pause_armed();
            const bool client_cron_armed = !srv_->flip_dispatch_paused() &&
                                           srv_->client_cron_armed();
            const bool client_lb_signal_armed = client_lb_signal_armed_;
            const bool lb_controller_armed = lb_controller_armed_;
            // Placement's dense role vectors are mutated only under FLIP's global dispatch
            // barrier. Do not consult them from an IO pass while that cold transaction is live.
            const bool save_cron_armed = !srv_->flip_dispatch_paused() &&
                                         srv_->save_cron_writer(self_->id());
            const bool client_cron_newly_armed = client_cron_armed && !client_cron_was_armed_;
            if (!client_cron_armed && __builtin_expect(client_cron_was_armed_, false)) {
                // Turning the last client cron consumer off also retires output accounting once.
                // The disabled write-back specialization then has no per-serve cleanup branch.
                for (Client* c : self_->clients()) c->stop_obuf_tracking();
            }
            client_cron_was_armed_ = client_cron_armed;
            sig.iterations++;
            reap_dead();               // free clients dead for a full iteration -- see close_client
            scatter_pool_.reap_deferred();

            uint32_t did = 0;
            bool submitted = false;
            bool natural_order = false;
            if constexpr (IoPipe)
                natural_order = iopipe_depth_gate_.loop_boundary(sig.ops);
            {
                Span busy(sig.busy_ns);
                // The work-span clock is already sampled once for this pass. Reuse that cut for
                // every monotonic millisecond consumer instead of issuing separate clock_gettime
                // reads for pause, cron and WAIT. A pass is microseconds; their public granularity
                // is milliseconds or seconds.
                bool pass_time_cached = pause_armed || client_cron_armed || save_cron_armed ||
                                        client_lb_signal_armed || lb_controller_armed ||
                                        !deferred_timers_.empty();
    // detach preserves the old race contract: a completion that lands while this batch is being
    // prepared can enqueue a fresh future visit.
    uint32_t wb_gather(WbBatch& batch) {
        if (batch.count) std::abort();
        if (pending_serve_.empty()) {
            aof_gate_target_ = 0;
            return 0;
        }

        AofManager& aof = srv_->aof();
        if (!aof_gate_target_) aof_gate_target_ = aof.posted_sequence();
        if (!aof.reply_gate_ready(aof_gate_target_)) {
            aof.register_send_gate_wait(self_->id());
            return 0;
        }
        aof_gate_target_ = 0;

        const size_t visits = std::min<size_t>(pending_serve_.size(),
                                               kIoPipeWbBatchClients);
        for (size_t i = 0; i < visits; i++) {
            Client* client = pending_serve_.front();
            pending_serve_.pop_front();
            client->set_serve_pending(false);
            if (!client->dead()) {
                batch.clients[batch.count] = client;
                batch.submit_allowed[batch.count] = true;
                batch.count++;
            }
        }
        return batch.count;
    }

    // WB.OBSERVE: consume completion hints, then gather the shallow pipeline's WB batch early so
    // its state/payload prefetch can overlap IFID work.
    template <bool HasUnix, bool kEp>
    uint32_t wb_observe(bool unmasked, WbBatch& batch) {
        return collect_retire_work<HasUnix, kEp>(unmasked) + wb_gather(batch);
    }

    // WB.PF pass 1 issues hints for every potentially retireable state line. Pass 2 performs the
    // required acquire and, only for a published plain BORROW, hints the store payload. The hint
    // neither reads nor copies payload bytes and never changes the borrow lifetime.
    void wb_prefetch(WbBatch& batch) {
        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < batch.count; i++) {
            Client* client = batch.clients[i];
            if (client->dead()) continue;
            Rob<kRobWindow>& rob = client->rob();
            const uint64_t first = rob.flush_id();
            const uint64_t last = rob.dispatch_id();
            const uint64_t count = std::min<uint64_t>(last - first,
                                                       kIoPipeWbPrefetchOpsPerClient);
            for (uint64_t off = 0; off < count; off++)
                __builtin_prefetch(&rob.at(first + off).state, 0, 3);
        }
        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < batch.count; i++) {
            Client* client = batch.clients[i];
            if (client->dead()) continue;
            Rob<kRobWindow>& rob = client->rob();
            const uint64_t first = rob.flush_id();
            const uint64_t last = rob.dispatch_id();
            const uint64_t count = std::min<uint64_t>(last - first,
                                                       kIoPipeWbPrefetchOpsPerClient);
            for (uint64_t off = 0; off < count; off++) {
                Op& op = rob.at(first + off);
                if (op.state.load(std::memory_order_acquire) != OpState::Done) break;
                if (!op.zc_ptr || op.zc_shard < 0 || !op.zc_len) continue;
                const uint32_t bytes = std::min(op.zc_len, kIoPipeWbBorrowPrefetchBytes);
                for (uint32_t pos = 0; pos < bytes; pos += kIoPipeCacheLineBytes)
                    __builtin_prefetch(op.zc_ptr + pos, 0, 1);
            }
        }
    }

    // IFID.RX: harvest this thread's wire completions/readiness, then select a bounded slice of the
    // independently maintained active set. In epoll mode the same tagged callback stream comes
    // from the doorbell mailbox before socket readiness is drained.
    template <bool HasUnix, bool HasTls, bool kEp>
    uint32_t ifid_rx(IfidBatch& batch) {
        uint32_t work = ring_.for_each_cqe(
            [&](io_uring_cqe* cqe) { on_cqe<HasTls, kEp, false, 1>(cqe); });
        if constexpr (kEp) work += epoll_pass<HasUnix, HasTls, false, 1>(0);
        if (batch.count) std::abort();
        const size_t available = active_.size();
        if (!available) { ifid_cursor_ = 0; return work; }
        if (ifid_cursor_ >= available) ifid_cursor_ = 0;
        const size_t visits = std::min<size_t>(available, kIoPipeIfidBatchClients);
        for (size_t i = 0; i < visits; i++) {
            Client* client = active_.at(ifid_cursor_);
            if (++ifid_cursor_ == available) ifid_cursor_ = 0;
            if (!client->dead()) batch.clients[batch.count++] = client;
        }
        return work;
    }

    // ---- IFID.PARSE+HASH: read-buffer maintenance, decode/hash/route, quiet publication --------
    template <bool HasTls, bool kEp, bool SplitLocal = false>
    uint32_t ifid_parse_hash(IfidBatch& batch) {
        uint32_t work = 0;
        backstop_pass_ = (++flush_tick_ >= kIoPipeWbBackstopTurns);
        if (backstop_pass_) flush_tick_ = 0;

        // The read side is one bounded batch before this rotation's retirement/send. Arming first
        // keeps the arrival stream flowing independently of the reply backlog.
        for (uint32_t batch_index = 0; batch_index < batch.count; batch_index++) {
            Client* c = batch.clients[batch_index];
            if (c->dead() || !c->in_active()) continue;
            Client& conn = *c;
            DispatchResult dispatch_result = DispatchResult::Progress;
            TlsConn* tls = nullptr;
            if constexpr (HasTls) tls = tls_engine(c);
            if (backstop_pass_ && !c->serve_pending()) enqueue_serve(c);

            if constexpr (HasTls) {
                if (tls) {
                    // Only the recv completion may drive inbound TLS while its BIO input frontier
                    // is pinned. Pipeline callbacks decrypt but defer parsing to this stage.
                    if (!c->closing() && !c->recv_armed())
                        (void)drive_tls<kEp, false, 1>(c);
                    else if (tls->userspace()) {
                        (void)wb_.pump_tls<kEp>(*c, *tls);
                        if (tls->socket_userspace() && tls->has_pinned_plain())
                            arm_tls_socket_poll<kEp>(c, tls->wanted());
                    }
                    tls = tls_engine(c);
                    if constexpr (kEp)
                        if (wb_.take_send_failure()) epoll_request_close(c);
                }
            }

            if (c->scatter_barrier()) {
                if (c->blocked() &&
                    blocking_resume_move(*srv_, *self_, ring_, *c, scatter_pool_)) {
                    enqueue_serve(c);
                    work++;
                }
                if (__builtin_expect(c->barrier_held_by(BarrierOwner::Debug), false) &&
                    !srv_->debug_barrier_hold_armed())
                    c->barrier_release(BarrierOwner::Debug);
                if (c->rob().quiesced()) c->barrier_release_quiesced();
            }
            if (c->atomic_backpressure() && srv_->atomic_can_admit(self_->id()) &&
                scatter_pool_.can_register_snapshot())
                c->set_atomic_backpressure(false);
            if (c->flip_backpressure() && !srv_->flip_dispatch_paused())
                c->set_flip_backpressure(false);
            if (c->rob().quiesced() && (kEp || !conn.recv_armed()))
                conn.reset_rbuf_at_quiescence();

            if constexpr (kEp) {
                if (c->closing()) c->set_recv_armed(false);
                if (!c->closing()) {
                    if constexpr (HasTls) {
                        if (tls) arm_tls_recv<kEp, false, 1>(c);
                        else arm_recv<kEp>(c);
                    } else {
                        arm_recv<kEp>(c);
                    }
                    if constexpr (HasTls) if (tls) {
                        (void)drive_tls<kEp, false, 1>(c);
                        tls = tls_engine(c);
                    }
                    if (wb_.take_send_failure()) epoll_request_close(c);
                }
            }

            if (!c->closing() && conn.rpos() < conn.rlen() && !c->scatter_barrier() &&
                !c->parse_backpressure()) {
                // The pause accounting and transport choice are the ordinary diet-era parse path;
                // only the 64-entry ROB-publication cap and deferred IFID.POST are schedule-specific.
                if (__builtin_expect(climon_pause_armed(), false)) {
                    const uint32_t rpos_before = conn.rpos();
                    if constexpr (HasTls) {
                        if (c->is_tls())
                            dispatch_result = parse_and_dispatch<true, 0, true, false, false, false, SplitLocal>(c);
                        else
                            dispatch_result = parse_and_dispatch<false, 0, true, false, false, false, SplitLocal>(c);
                    } else {
                        dispatch_result = parse_and_dispatch<false, 0, true, false, false, false, SplitLocal>(c);
                    }
                    if (conn.rpos() != rpos_before) work++;
                } else {
                    if constexpr (HasTls) {
                        if (c->is_tls())
                            dispatch_result = parse_and_dispatch<true, 0, true, false, false, false, SplitLocal>(c);
                        else
                            dispatch_result = parse_and_dispatch<false, 0, true, false, false, false, SplitLocal>(c);
                    } else {
                        dispatch_result = parse_and_dispatch<false, 0, true, false, false, false, SplitLocal>(c);
                    }
                    if (__builtin_expect(dispatch_result != DispatchResult::NeedInput, true))
                        work++;
                }
            }

            if constexpr (!kEp) {
                if constexpr (HasTls) {
                    if (tls && tls->memory_bio()) arm_tls_recv<kEp, false, 1>(c);
                    else if (!tls) arm_recv<kEp>(c);
                } else {
                    arm_recv<kEp>(c);
                }
            }

            const bool stuck = (conn.rpos() < conn.rlen() && c->rob().full()) ||
                               (!conn.recv_armed() && !c->closing());
            const bool more_input = conn.rpos() < conn.rlen() &&
                                    dispatch_result != DispatchResult::NeedInput;
            const bool tls_output = tls && (tls->output_pending() || c->send_inflight());
            const bool done = c->rob().quiesced() && !more_input && !stuck &&
                              !c->serve_pending() && c->nothing_to_write() && !tls_output;
            // Batch entries remain readable through the existing corpse grace; membership is the
            // authoritative check before mutating the active set.
            if (c->dead() || !c->in_active()) continue;
            if (done && !c->closing()) {
                c->set_in_active(false);
                active_.erase(c);
            } else if (c->closing() && !tls_output && c->safe_to_release()) {
                if (pubsub_disconnect_ready(c)) {
                    c->set_in_active(false);
                    active_.erase(c);
                    close_client(c);
                }
            }
        }

        if constexpr (kEp) {
            while (!epoll_closes_.empty()) {
                Client* victim = epoll_closes_.back();
                epoll_closes_.pop_back();
                epoll_close_now(victim);
            }
        }
        // The IO role drains only its local-read lane. All writes and demotions still use
        // the ordinary split owner inbox; publish QSBR only after every capture is consumed.
        if constexpr (SplitLocal) work += fused_executor_->split_read_local_pass();
        return work;
    }

    // IFID.POST: quiet queue tails are already published. Fold their notification/wake edge once
    // per destination, then preserve the existing pub/sub parse-to-send boundary.
    uint32_t ifid_post(IfidBatch&) {
        uint32_t work = flush_ifid_posts();
        if (__builtin_expect(pubsub_pass_pending_, false)) work += pubsub_pass_flush();
        return work;
    }

    // WB.RETIRE+PREP: drain only the in-order Done prefix and construct reply buffers/iovecs. The
    // engine methods are the ordinary serve bodies with their final pump deliberately omitted.
    template <bool HasTls, bool kEp, bool Coded = false>
    uint32_t wb_retire_prepare(WbBatch& batch) {
        uint32_t work = 0;
        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < batch.count; i++) {
            Client* c = batch.clients[i];
            if (c->dead()) continue;
            if (__builtin_expect((climon_armed_cached_ & Server::kClimonReply) != 0, false) &&
                climon_reply_suppressed(c)) {
                work += climon_prepare_suppressed(c, batch.submit_allowed[i]);
                continue;
            }
            if constexpr (HasTls) {
                if (TlsConn* tls = tls_engine(c)) {
                    if (wb_.prepare_tls<kEp, Coded>(*c, *tls, batch.submit_allowed[i])) work++;
                    if (tls->failed()) close_client(c, tls->output_pending() || c->send_inflight());
                } else if (TlsConn* slot = tls_slot_conn(c); slot && slot->ktls()) {
                    if (wb_.prepare_ktls<kEp, Coded>(*c, batch.submit_allowed[i])) work++;
                } else if (wb_.prepare<kEp, Coded>(*c, batch.submit_allowed[i])) {
                    work++;
                }
            } else if (wb_.prepare<kEp, Coded>(*c, batch.submit_allowed[i])) {
                work++;
            }
        }
        return work;
    }

    // WB.SUBMIT+RECLAIM: form the actual sends from the warm prepared batch. Send completion
    // reclamation stays at the next rotation's RX/CQE boundary.
    template <bool HasTls, bool kEp>
    uint32_t wb_submit_reclaim(WbBatch& batch, bool& submitted) {
        uint32_t work = 0;
        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < batch.count; i++) {
            Client* c = batch.clients[i];
            if (c->dead() || !batch.submit_allowed[i]) continue;
            if constexpr (HasTls) {
                if (TlsConn* tls = tls_engine(c)) {
                    if (wb_.pump_tls<kEp>(*c, *tls)) work++;
                    if (tls->socket_userspace() && tls->has_pinned_plain())
                        arm_tls_socket_poll<kEp>(c, tls->wanted());
                    if (tls->failed()) close_client(c, tls->output_pending() || c->send_inflight());
                } else if (wb_.pump<kEp>(*c)) {
                    work++;
                }
            } else if (wb_.pump<kEp>(*c)) {
                work++;
            }
            if constexpr (kEp)
                if (wb_.take_send_failure()) epoll_close_now(c);
        }
        // The source schedule's early fire point is preserved. The live liburing query replaces
        // its shadow pending counter, so the diet keeps zero work at individual SQE producers.
        if constexpr (!kEp) {
            if (ring_.sq_ready()) {
                ring_.submit_and_reap();
                submitted = true;
            }
        }
        return work;
    }

    // At depth, completed IFID work already provides the latency-hiding window. Retain the plain
    // split loop's combined retire/stage/pump order and skip the separate WB prefetch walks.
    template <bool HasTls, bool kEp, bool Coded = false>
    uint32_t wb_serve_natural(WbBatch& batch, bool& submitted) {
        uint32_t work = 0;
        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < batch.count; i++) {
            Client* c = batch.clients[i];
            if (c->dead()) continue;
            if (__builtin_expect((climon_armed_cached_ & Server::kClimonReply) != 0, false) &&
                climon_reply_suppressed(c)) {
                work += climon_serve_suppressed(c);
                if constexpr (kEp)
                    if (wb_.take_send_failure()) epoll_close_now(c);
                continue;
            }
            if constexpr (HasTls) {
                if (TlsConn* tls = tls_engine(c)) {
                    if (wb_.serve_tls<kEp, false, Coded>(*c, *tls)) work++;
                    if (tls->socket_userspace() && tls->has_pinned_plain())
                        arm_tls_socket_poll<kEp>(c, tls->wanted());
                    if (tls->failed()) close_client(c, tls->output_pending() || c->send_inflight());
                } else if (TlsConn* slot = tls_slot_conn(c); slot && slot->ktls()) {
                    if (wb_.serve_ktls<kEp, false, Coded>(*c)) work++;
                } else if (wb_.serve<kEp, false, Coded>(*c)) {
                    work++;
                }
            } else if (wb_.serve<kEp, false, Coded>(*c)) {
                work++;
            }
            if constexpr (kEp)
                if (wb_.take_send_failure()) epoll_close_now(c);
        }
        if constexpr (!kEp) {
            if (ring_.sq_ready()) {
                ring_.submit_and_reap();
                submitted = true;
            }
        }
        return work;
    }

    template <bool HasUnix, bool HasTls, bool kEp, bool SplitLocal = false>
    uint32_t pipeline_pass(bool unmasked, bool natural_order, bool& submitted) {
        srv_->mode_schedule_stats(self_->id()).note_overlap(
            OverlapSchedule::SplitIo, !natural_order);

        // and kernel SQEs own their data after their stage, so no ping/pong lifetime is required.
        IfidBatch& ifid = ifid_batch_;

                    case IoPipeStage::IfidRx:

                        break;
                    case IoPipeStage::WbPrefetch:

                    case IoPipeStage::IfidParseHash:

                    case IoPipeStage::WbRetirePrepare:
                        work += wb_retire_prepare<HasTls, kEp, SplitLocal>(wb);
                        break;
                    case IoPipeStage::IfidPost:
                        work += ifid_post(ifid);
                        break;
                    case IoPipeStage::WbSubmitReclaim:
                        work += wb_submit_reclaim<HasTls, kEp>(wb, submitted);
